utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, for the record from the Defence teams I notice the absence of Mr. Ostojic and Mr. Haynes. Present for the Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Nicholls. There are a couple of things that we needed to draw your attention to. I'm addressing Prosecution in particular and for the first item. Yesterday, I think the Pandurevic Defence team filed a motion requesting their own expert who is named in the motion, I don't need to repeat the name, to be present during the testimony of your expert witness Butler. Do you have any objection to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good afternoon. None at all, Your Honour. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we are disposing of the motion orally here and now. Motion is being granted for two reasons. One, because the request is, in our opinion, justified, and secondly, because the Prosecution adheres to the request. Yesterday also the Prosecution filed a motion requesting to amend the 65 ter exhibit list relating to Witness number 2, Dean Manning. Now, as you know Dean Manning is scheduled to start his testimony on Monday. I don't know if you are in a position today, if you're not, we are establishing a deadline, that being Friday for your responses. If there is opposition, please let us know now so that we can grant the motion and -- Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We respond to that motion, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. So Friday, please, is the latest, so that Monday when we return we'll be in a position to dispose of the motion. Similarly, today the Defence filed a motion request the determination of the evidence of the same witness, of Dean Manning. Again, we cannot allow for -- for the usual procedural time limit in this case because he starts on Monday. So we are also giving you up till Friday to file your response, and then we'll dispose of the two motions first thing Monday morning. Okay. Then there are other matters. I think our Senior Legal Officer will be approaching those who are directly related. One deals with the Pandurevic motion, and the other one deals with the Miletic motion. All right. Having said that, I think if there are no further preliminaries on your part we can bring in the witness. Yes? Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, to you, Mr. Petrovic, and welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will resume the examination-in-chief, and then we'll proceed with the cross-examinations. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just for the record, I note that Mr. Petrovic has brought some papers with him. I don't know exactly what they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One a moment, one moment. Okay. It was my fault, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I notice the witness, Mr. Petrovic, has some papers with him. I don't have any objection, I just want to make sure my friends to know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but let me explain to the witness because we need to be fair with everyone here. Mr. Petrovic, the procedure here is as follows: You are allowed to refer to notes that you may have made and documents that you may bring with you in the course of your testimony, especially if you need to refresh your memory or consult your records. However, however, you need to be aware that if you do so, then either parties, both Prosecution and Defence can ask to see those papers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So I'm just explaining what the procedure is. So in other words, if you make use of them, then you have to make them available if a request is made.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For example, information for my subpoena among other things, but they're free to -- I can offer them to see this. No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So, yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to pick up where we left off -- where we left off yesterday, sir, and part of what I was asking you about was the chronology of your meetings with Mr. Borovcanin and you told us how you were embedded in his unit in 1994, and we all know about the time you spent with him in July 1995. What I'd like to do is ask you now when was the next time you met Mr. Borovcanin after 15 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in my village near Belgrade, beginning 2002, I think. Anyway, sometime after he was, as I heard, in contact with you, and he decided to -- to come to The Hague. So he wanted me to -- to testify for him for the -- it is as I counted more or less in all 40 hours. So for those 40 hours I had no -- no reason not to say it's not only help for him, but I think also for this Tribunal, for the final truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And what did you say to Mr. Borovcanin when you met him at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This meeting was very short. I just agreed right away. I don't remember details. The essential was done by me in the first minute of our talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And after that, did you meet with Mr. Borovcanin's Defence lawyers or investigators working for him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I met with your colleague Mr. McCloskey, and I met with -- he will be angry now, the lawyer from the team, Mr. Lazarevic. He's from Bijeljina if I know well, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now I want to ask you, before we get into talking about those 40 hours with Mr. Borovcanin, can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I apologise to my colleague. I believe there is a huge misunderstanding here about these 40 hours. Maybe it has to do with two events happening at the same time. I don't believe -- I don't know how to proceed now. The witness obviously does speak very good English. On the other hand, I can make my submission in B/C/S but he would understand it anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can re-ask my question which might --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Even if you ask Mr. Bourgon or Ms. Fauveau -- yeah. Anyway --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can ask it a different way, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think that would solve the problem. If it doesn't, we will have submissions in the absence of the witness and we'll carry on from there. Yes, Mr. -- Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic and thank you, Mr. Nicholls and thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Later on I'm going to ask you some more about the time you spent with Mr. Borovcanin on the 12th and the 13th of July, 1995, but right now what I want to ask you about is what you did with your raw footage that you shot that you shared with us and how you turned that into the documentary that was broadcast on Studio B. Just if you can briefly explain what you did with your 8-millimetre tape when you came back to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do what was my work for. I agreed with the editor-in-chief to do a documentary. I returned and I started editing from the machines they have, because it's not professional machine, and I am not professional cameraman. I'm pretty lousy cameraman. Good journalist, but bad cameraman. So it came to -- first to Studio B.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when did your -- well, could you tell us the title of your documentary?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Title in Serbian is Operacija Srebrenica, it means Operation Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 28 minutes document, which is in standard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when did that programme air on Studio B? When was it played?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Few days later. 15th of -- maybe even that night or 17th. I mixed all the time the -- but it was right after we did it. We started right away when we returned, and we aired as quick as possible. So in two, three days' time after airing everybody was interested by the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Would you like to know the date you gave us in the interview? Would that help you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, maybe 15 or 17th something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You told us 17th.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 17th, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just try to think about it while we go on.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a long time ago, so one day more or less, it's not important to the story.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to play just the very, very beginning. We're not going to watch the whole thing by any means at this time. 2011 the Studio B documentary, just so the witness can see what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think that's enough, and I think you probably remember that. What have we just been watching?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want me to tell you what we are watching?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. I have to ask questions in a certain way, so I have to ask you what that is rather than telling you --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is -- I respected mostly the -- the realtime in the -- in the moments I got there, so this is in raw material also the real beginning of the pictures I did coming -- coming to the British -- pardon, the Dutch compound in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you just confirm that what we just saw was the beginning of your documentary?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in addition to that 28-minute documentary for Studio B --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's 28 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did you write any articles about this --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: These events?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These articles, you have it in your documentation also and everybody. It was an interview magazine from Belgrade which doesn't exist anymore, six years. In that time -- it's Politika Editing House, and it was the story, the same thing but with more details, because I think my -- my printed reportage was better than with the documentary because of my principal problem not good knowledge of manipulating camera and not good camera at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand. And just since you've brought that up, I don't think you answered that yesterday. Was that a professional camera or was that a personal camera? What was that you were using?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a camera I bought once in 1993 in New York. It costed maybe $750 and it last -- it's destiny, it was stolen from Studio B once when they wanted to repair it, so they owe me money for this also.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember the date that your article was published in Interview Magazine?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it recently I think the date is 21st of July or something. End of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we bring up 469, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 21st.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we're looking at your article; is that right? Thank you. You've just told us that you were I think happier with the article than with the --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Professionally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. And you said yesterday about how your -- your previous article when you were embedded the first time with Mr. Borovcanin's unit was objective and earned you credit. How do you feel about this article you published on the 21st in terms of its objectivity, its balance, its accuracy? If you could describe it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm pretty sure that even today that it was one of the most -- of the best articles explaining the situation after entering of Serbs in Srebrenica, because I applied in -- in most of the moments of this text very documentary things that I wrote, like I writing this here now about the Tribunal. The notes, I don't made them -- I didn't make them more beautiful afterwards. I have a technique since beginning to -- to have a fidelity to my initial text which is in the -- in the notes. So this -- this I applied, and everything what was said there, most of the statements, this is what I heard around. I mean, quotations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you this: The notes you're referring to that you used as a basis for your article, did you write those down on the 13th and 14th of July or did you write them down from your memory after you got back from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of them I cannot be so specific, but probably some of -- some of notes in parts -- in moments when I didn't film, because if you compare this text with the film, you will see also different scenes that I don't have on picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand. Now --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was alone. That's why, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, the last thing I want to do is -- and to let you know, the Trial Chamber has viewed a copy of the material that you provided with us at your interview which we called the raw material, and I want to show you some parts of that and have you comment on those parts, just whether they were in the original, whether it's something that's been taped over or just how these little clips got into the raw material, if you can. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. We will play the first one. These are from -- 2054 is the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I do it alone, the second button?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. That's good. That was a clip at 08:58:4 of a shell casing after the house with the belongings in front of it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just if you can tell us about --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This shell is still in my -- on the balcony at my home. This shell is from 1991, from Vukovar battlefield. And -- and it proves also that this unfortunate raw material was, as I said, previously like folk song, you know. It was in many hands. And even there I don't remember I filmed, but this cassette -- this 8-millimetres cassette was used many times. So it was not profession -- it was not for professional use, which is -- there is a custom to -- to tape only once. And this was used for many purposes and many times, so this material you -- you talk about -- you're talking about is not so reliable, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For expertise, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's why -- excuse me. That's why I since the beginning thought that my 28 minutes is the most just and most accurate material about this subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a couple more. Your explanation may be the same or it may not. It's -- we'll see.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's about Karadzic scene there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's one of them.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We'll play the next one, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe -- excuse me. Maybe it's a moment I promise to lady translators to speak in one language. So if I have to choose between English and Europe, one of the old European languages which is Serbian, I would prefer now to continue in Serb if you permit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's perfectly fine.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have the right to choose your own language.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Anytime, whichever you prefer. Okay. We're starting at 10 minutes, 15 seconds?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am not seeing anything at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That -- excuse me. That's correct. This clip is a part of the tape where the screen goes blank, but you can hear -- you can't hear it at the moment unfortunately, for some reason, but you can hear the text which is -- here we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you can just -- if you have any comments on that.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] this is most probably, as I can see it -- the sound has been amplified. I've never paid any attention to it. This is probably my house, a conversation with somebody on that occasion. This was a topic that was of some interest for many people, and I can't provide any other comment. This is just something that was recorded by way of interference. I really can't tell you after such a long time about the context within which this was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. The third one you'll be familiar with. I just wanted to show it to you. It is a box of military rations it looks like. You'll see it in a minute. Now starting at 24:10 we started.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is again a part of my old machine which pre-dated the computer era in my country. I didn't have a computer. And this is proof that NATO was involved in helping the Mujahedin, like I told you yesterday. Around Majevica NATO shared food with the Mujahedin, and I brought that information as a tidbit from my journey, and I would show these clips all over the place in Serbia. This is yet another proof that this cassette had been used and reused, and I really don't know why this happened, how come the film that you want to show has been interrupted. I know which direction this is taking, but I can't take you any more than that. I am -- I recognise the NATO standard portions that were used to feed volunteers from the Muslim world who came to Bosnia to bring us closer to the European Union. And if you will allow me, this was a bit of a cynicism, because you asked for it didn't you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know when that little clip we've seen of the -- of the ration box, the food box, was filmed, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I cannot, because it is connected with the previous times. I brought this from some of the fronts right before Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it's simply -- maybe it's in Pale maybe on some the front I was. It's very difficult to tell you. I don't know. Tell me more I will tell you eventually more. I don't know what you want to prove.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, no. I'm just trying to get your best memory of when that might have happened.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oops, I started again in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's okay. Let me see if I understood you. Do you know if that was taped before or after July 1995, the box?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's probably because of the box. The first talk in the family must be in the same occasion or -- but I cannot prove. But it must be before because I had this much before Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The last one is the one you referred to, Mr. Karadzic. We'll just play it for one second. It's at 23:21 we're starting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. [Interpretation] This short clip, maybe a second or two, that again is from that same cassette that we're talking about. This is raw material, and it is obvious this was done in the studio of Television Pale preceding Dr. Karadzic's interview, and this was attended by a team of TF1 television that I had brought, that I had very often used during the war, and they recorded that as -- to be shown, because they needed something that was recorded on the ground. I was with them, and this was taken when I entered that studio with the French, and they also recorded this interview with Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, is that on the tape before you go to Srebrenica in mid-July or after? When does it get on the tape, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] It could be -- [Interpretation] If I could check with the French team when they were there, I could tell you. After Srebrenica, I couldn't go to Bosnia, because I received threats because of this video. So this could have been in 1994, prior to Srebrenica, because I also authored two long interviews with Dr. Karadzic, one for Television Belgrade, and it was also aired on Studio B Television. On reflection, I believe that this was before July 1995. But you have to bear in mind that that cassette was used by poor people. There were no cameras. There was no money for videotapes, and that's why this cassette was used and reused, which resulted in a bit of chaos. The whole problem arises from the fact that I gave this cassette to everybody, which must be a unique case in the professional journalism towards the end of the 20th century. I don't think there is any similar case anywhere. That's the explanation. These are several layers intertwining, very short clips interfering on a videotape that was used and reused many times to put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. But just to make sure I understand, you said the tape was shared with many other people, but the clips we've seen, if I understood you, you took yourself in Pale on your balcony or did I get that wrong?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now I want to move to the 13th of July. You told us about how you met Mr. Borovcanin on the bridge in Bratunac and the procedure of how you crossed the bridge. Could you -- and then I think you told us as well that you went straight to Potocari. Who was in the car with you when you went to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Mr. Borovcanin met me, I had my own car on the Serb side of the bridge, i.e., of the Drina River. On the other bank was Mr. Borovcanin in a car, and in that car we went -- actually, for a long time I could not remember whether we were on our own. I believe that we went to the compound on our own, the two of us, and that later on a driver joined us, somebody from the police probably. Your colleague kept on saying that I was always in some military or police vehicle, military vehicle, rather, which is just nonsense. I would like him to show me a photo of that vehicle. I was with Borovcanin who was police, not the army. We came after Bratunac. We passed through Bratunac. At the far end of Bratunac there was this compound, and the first shots taken from the car depict that. We pulled over somewhere there and we proceeded on foot. You will see later some people arriving there, and it is more than clear that the shots were taken from -- not from a car but by me standing on the ground. Is there anything else you would like me to tell you? A little bit more -- [In English] Translators again. Am I too fast?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think you're okay. They will alert you if you're going too fast?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't agree with you, Mr. Nicholls. I think if he continues in Serbian, I think it would be better for the interpreters, because the moment you are both speaking English you are tending to overlap.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the lady interpreters whether they are able to follow me, i.e., whether I am slow enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think if we go at this pace, the way that you're talking and the way I'm talking, we will be fine. Do you remember -- can you describe the car you drove in with Mr. Borovcanin when you went to Potocari, the colour --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. It was just a car. It was nothing special. It was just an ordinary passenger vehicle. Not Yugoslav made. It was probably a Japanese-made car because it was already that time when we had some imports from Japan. I really don't know. You will have to somebody -- somebody. I didn't pay much attention to the cars that I was driven in, but it was not a military car. If Mr. Ruez is listening, I would really like him to explain how could he speak such a load of nonsense which is absolutely inadmissible for a level that he was at.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I think you've made clear. Who was driving the car on the way to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] On the way to Potocari. I think it was Mr. Borovcanin, but maybe again I'm wrong. In this period of this story -- [Interpretation] I apologise once again. It may have been the driver who had been sent. I really can't recollect his presence from the bridge to the entrance to the compound, and I really hope you can't expect me to remember that. I was -- concentrated more on the events and not the car that I was being driven in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does he remember the colour of the car?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think I asked that, if he could describe the colour, and he said absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has given us an indication that it was probably Japanese. Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judging by the length of the car, I believe that it was a medium-sized car. It was not very luxurious. I can't remember the colour despite my efforts. I would very much like to be able to tell you something about the car, but I can't. I don't even remember that I put it in my text, the colour of the car. But I know that not for a single moment was I in any contact with the military or their vehicles if that is the ultimate drift of your question. I spent all my time with Mr. Borovcanin, who was a member of the special police of that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me -- let me just say something to you. This isn't a question. I'm not trying to trick you. I wasn't trying to get -- get you to say it was a military car. I was asking you just if you remembered the car and if you could describe it, and that's completely all I was asking.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you the truth. I really can't remember the detail of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you've made it clear you don't remember whether there was a driver in the car with you and Mr. Borovcanin at the beginning or at Potocari, and you've just said, "I spent all my time with Mr. Borovcanin, who was a member of the special police of that brigade." Was there any time you were in that car driving without Mr. Borovcanin in the video we see?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the video footage that I aired, that at the time Mr. Borovcanin was with me or the other way round, I was with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And you've explained a little bit about what it means to be embedded in a unit and how you had difficulty getting to Srebrenica first because of the conflict and that you could have been arrested. Was there any agreement with Mr. Borovcanin or with anybody about what you would -- not what you would film, but what you would do, where you would be during your time there with Mr. Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm a journalist, and Mr. Borovcanin participated in the war. He was a warrior. Every journalist is looking for exclusive piece of news. Let me explain that. My colleague, a Serbian journalist, tried to enter Mosul in 2003 in Iraq, but he wasn't embedded with the Americans. He could not come close to them. I'm talking about Mr. Lazanski. If you know what war is, especially the modern war, if you don't have passage, if you're not there you can't get any news because modern armies do not recognise journalism as such. That's why I had tried to look for ways and means and one of them was to call people that I knew. If I had known somebody else from the army, from the military, for example, I would have asked them, although the military probably would not have allowed me to enter because it was their general position that the operation was under way, and I could see that when I was there. During my short stay I could see that the fighting was still going on and it would still go on for days. This is the kind of situation in which you're seeking opportunities to get in. How do you get in if an operation was under way? And I was able to find a way. The man believed me, he trusted me. He thought that there was nothing to hide from me. I suppose that he would have had a lot less problems if this film had never been made, but life is a bitch, and he's now in -- in the prison. This is not the classical explanation of the word "embedded" in this case. He trusted me. I came upon his invitation, and I could do things because I was with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to show you another clip. This is from the Studio B footage, 2011, and it's a -- you'll recognise this immediately, sir. It's a shot of men on a balcony. You'll see in a minute.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just threw a glance on the previous page. I would like to clarify something in the interpretation. Maybe this has been happening often. When I was talking about my colleague, the Serb journalist who tried to enter, I said Mosul in Iraq. This is a very important thing. He could not enter there. And if you look at the transcript, you can't see where he tried to enter. I tried to explain to you what does it mean to be embedded in today's day and age, and if you don't see it precisely on the transcript, I'm sure that there are some other imprecisions. And if you will continue being so imprecise, then I will speak English. This is inadmissible. I'm sure that I will same some other even more important things, and if they are going to be imprecise I don't want to go on speaking Serbian. And just one more question. If I continue speaking Serbian, can I see that version on the screen as well, my words in Serbian on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please slow down, both of you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please slow down, both of you, and let's proceed in as calm a manner as possible, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me just explain something to you, Mr. Petrovic. This is a rough transcript which is made by our very good people here right as we go along. Sometimes there's a symbol, it's like an upside down V?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that means that that is a part to check particularly carefully. Everyone of these transcripts is listened to over and over again before it becomes the final transcript, but it's impossible to get a perfect transcript simultaneously. So nothing in this world is perfect. Occasionally there may be mistakes. But you don't need to worry that what you see here is the way that this is going into the record permanently.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. I will try and slow down so that Mosul and Iraq may be recorded, because this is important, and these are not some unknown names, but I appreciate what you have just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let's play the clip. This is at 2:30. This is again actually from our compilation trial video, but it's the same clip from the Studio B. If we could play this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The first question: What did you learn, if anything, on the spot there in the front of the house when you were filming these men about who they were and why they were up there on the balcony?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is sentence from the final version in the programme, this is the voice off, which belongs to the over all information that I gathered here and there during my filming, and after my return I inquired with various people. There are people who had studied crimes committed over the Serbs as well. So that as a conscientious journalist, I took my task seriously, and the task was to provide the general public with as much information as possible, and this is one of the sentences that I put in the text, because, one, the programme was edited, once the material was edited, and when you append sound to it then I read the text. In a normal television houses, in rich television houses, it would be different. In my case, I had a microphone in my hand. I was watching the clip, and I was commenting in the studio. Some parts of the video clip, however, contained my voice online. For example, the Dutch doctor officer who was there whom I'd asked what was going on. That's how things are done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. My question is: When did you learn that these men on the balcony, or when were you told that these men on the balcony were criminals or suspected criminals who had tried to get onto the convoys? When did you learn that piece of information?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This may be due to two things or two things are possible. I might have heard this. In that chaos I heard it from people while people were being assisted with their departure to Tuzla, people from Srebrenica, and I may have also investigated things as soon as I returned learned it while I was editing the programme. It is only logical that I heard it from somebody there while I was filming, but I can't remember the details. You have to know that I have to remember the words and record. These are two different things, and you can't be equally successful at both. So I really can't be very precise in answering this question. I can't tell you when I heard it or from whom. I didn't know anybody but Mr. Borovcanin for that matter, but I suppose that I put a question, somebody answered the question. I did not record it. And I believe that I actually got this information from the ground, from where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: At the time you were filming?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Most probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, you say probably. Let me -- let me just ask if you remember what you said in our interview when we met in 2006. That was earlier.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember what you told me then?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically -- [Interpretation] Can you jog my memory, please? Can you quote the exact text? This must be in the -- in the -- in the material that you gave me to read yesterday or the day before. I can't remember all the details on the 200 pages of the text that you showed me yesterday and the interview took place a year and a half ago, didn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's understandable. The question was on page 172. "How did you come to the conclusion that these people on the balcony, they should be screened for war crimes?" And your answer was: "This is not my conclusion. This is something I heard on the spot. I don't remember who said. I probably asked somebody."

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is very similar to the answer that I have just provided. I don't see any contradiction between that, what I told you a year and a half ago, and what I've just told you now. The long and the short of it is that I can't really be sure of who provided that information to me. Was it John or Peter or Paul, but this was said to me. I saw people on the balcony, and I knew who they were. I am not a warrior. I was a journalist and it was my duty to convey information, and that information could have been rumour, could have been objective or subjective but it was not my conclusion in any case. This is something that I heard. And it had -- it had a very clear purpose in the programme. It would have been a logical explanation that they were being looked for and that's -- they were separated there. Somebody in the compound probably answered that question. Nobody volunteered any information. I always put question, but I don't know who I saw, because I had a dual role to play. I had the role to ask questions and to record at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall hearing at any time then about this time that you were there about lists of criminals?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that. There is a researcher in Belgrade, Mr. Ivanisevic, who is a well-respected researcher, a very pedantic person. His wife hails from Srebrenica and he is familiar with the people there. The agency that I worked for, Belgrade-based news agency called Bina, as early as 1994 we published a publication about war crimes, and his first list of crimes from Podrinje, and this was in English. The regime in Belgrade you have to know at the time as of 1993, of May 1993, up to 1995 carried out very strict censorship of everything that arrived from Republika Srpska. As a result of all those things --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So -- let me just finish. Ivanisevic has that list and maybe I had that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. The question was just about at the time. Do you recall what you wrote about the -- about the police knowing the names of criminals in your article which you published on the 21st of July based on your notes which you took?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It did not only involve the notes. We're go back to the information, to my personal knowledge as a journalist. One doesn't go out into the field with zero knowledge, blindfolded. Of course you have to prepare beforehand. In my luggage I had had information, because back in 1994 I had published a book on those crimes and there was a list of people there. Besides one of the persons indicted for war crimes was on the list that I gave to Mr. McCloskey when he was in Belgrade, and that individual was mentioned in Ivanisevic's book. Now he's a member of the Social Democratic Party down there in Srebrenica. He was on that list too. Now, when I tell you that these individuals were, well, this means that I had personal knowledge about the Serbs having had information on the individuals who had been plundering in the area for two years. You have to know that more than 6.000 houses, Serb houses, were torched and destroyed, and 2.500 people were killed, and this is something that is never talked about. I didn't pay particular attention to that fact. It was merely an illustration and I repeated that story in the magazine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, you did. And just to make sure I'm clear, then, when you wrote in the article that the Serb police moved in Potocari had the names of all the criminals, you knew that before you went there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you repeat your question once more, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You gave a very long answer so I'm trying to clarify. I don't if my friend is standing up or not. He's going up and down. What I want to know is that if you had this information that the Serb police in Potocari had the names of Muslim criminals there before you arrived or not.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not have been able to have that sort of information. Do not try and lead me into these waters. I am a journalist. Who would provide such a piece of information to a journalist? Did you ever see Americans releasing the information on how many of their soldiers had been -- or people had been killed in Iraq? Well, they never released that. Mr. Borovcanin is neither my brother or relative. I was not a member of their army either. I was a foreign citizen -- citizen from another country. He found me likable and respected me, but to provide that sort of information to someone in the midst of a war, that would be nonsense.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you again in a different way. Try to listen very carefully to my question because I wasn't asking you whether you got that information from Mr. Borovcanin. That wasn't part of my question. Let me just ask you this: Would it help you to look at the paragraph you wrote about this in your article on the -- which was published on the 21st of July? Would you like to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we could look at 469, please, page 2. Well, page 2 in English, which is -- I'm sorry, I don't have all of this synchronised, but I believe he could -- I believe the witness could read it just fine in English. It's probably page 1 of the original. Actually, probably page 2 of the original as well. On the English, on page 2, the fourth paragraph down -- the third paragraphs talks about as you were telling us crimes committed by Muslims against Serb civilians, and then the paragraph I want you to find and read begins: "Jevic and the other policemen know that only too well. They have the names of all the criminals. And in this jungle of people, children in tears, dirty bundles, dust and the unbearable stench and certain other smells they seem -- they have to find these specimens as well among the Muslim civilians, and indeed there seem to have been some, at least among the ones that were peeping from the balcony of one building near the UN base."

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now we're discussing the text that I wrote as soon as I finished my programme. It was also written in a very short period of time. It had its dynamic. I had this load of information, including names of certain individuals. And if I saw that the person had anything to do with the operation, I combined that information with the information that could not have been refuted in any way by that point, and that was of course Mr. Ivanisevic, because he had the largest list of all the criminals in that area, which is the area of Podrinje, the Drina valley. That's the -- that particular curve of the Drina. So that's a scenario of a text speaking about a war event.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. The part you read out -- I read out, this paragraph about Jevic and the other policemen knowing about the criminals and that there were some peering through the balcony, is that something that you knew, that you heard, or something that you logically came to after reading about other lists and putting together pieces of picture or something -- or is that something that you knew to be true when you wrote your article?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's probably the combination of my presence on the very spot where I filmed the people on the balcony and the previous knowledge arising from the information and the list by Mr. Ivanisevic, and this corresponded. The two corresponded, in my mind. And to the reader, it was quite clear that -- they could infer logically that they had those lists there on the spot. I can't tell you where I heard it or who I heard it from. I might have heard some of the information there. I combined all these various pieces of information with the existing list from the book of Mr. Ivanisevic, which had been published a year before, and it was already in existence and it could account for many things that became known later. I can't, however, tell you whether it was Pero who told me this or that. I am giving you the names that I heard out there --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- on the spot, but I cannot quote or cite anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: On this page --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or I apologise. Let me give you this illustration: On this page I can see one portion of the text that I was unable to check. We can see the photograph, and below it says "Abdic." He was one of the Muslim leaders who was supposed to avert the war, but he was unable to overpower Izetbegovic. This is something that I probably would never publish today, but I didn't have the time, the fact that this -- that he was seen there with the Serbs. This is a very interesting piece of information in view of the later developments in Srebrenica. Why am I telling you this? Because I tied this up with the scene that I witnessed on my way back to Belgrade on that very same bridge, where I saw the French, Russian, and Yugoslav Colonels on their way to a meeting with Mladic. And as a journalist, I linked up all these things. They all avoided saying anything. And the function of this text was to indicate all the goings-on and that this was of course within the bare minimum that I had with which I tried to receive the maximum.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Do you know a man named Dusko Jevic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [English] I heard about him -- [Interpretation] I heard about him 12 but he is not an acquaintance of mine. I did not come across him. Perhaps I 13 saw him earlier on in relation to that brigade, but I can't say that I got to know him nearly as well as I did Mr. Borovcanin, for instance. So, I do not remember him except from that text when I wrote down some of the names that I had heard. Therefore, we -- one can't say that we were acquaintances.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. This is quite the simple question. Did you, if you recall, see Dusko Jevic in Potocari on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. I can't tell you precisely. I probably did see him. But you know what sort of encounters this was. In passing, because I was filming all the time going back and forth, left and right. I needed as much time as I could to shoot as many frames as I was able to because I was not a cameraman. If I saw him, the encounter last for a couple of seconds. I don't recall being with him in the same situation that I was with when I was filming Mr. Borovcanin with the members of the UNPROFOR. I don't recall ever being in such a scene with that individual whereas I do remember these other scenes. I would probably also have filmed him. That's why I'm thinking it's not possible for me to reproduce this to you in an authentic manner. Indeed, the scene was such that this was absolutely insignificant to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. You've answered that question. I'd like to show you something now. It's an another short video clip. This is 2991. Again, this is -- you'll see about the men on the balcony that you filmed. This is something I'll tell you in advance that we created here by looking at --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- your Studio B film and the raw materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. The --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The Studio B footage on the clip 2991 was the one on the left --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Left.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- you could tell. The raw material which you kindly provided to us was on the right. And you can see perhaps -- well, I won't need -- I'll ask you. Do you think -- what do you think was on that bit of film now that you look at this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean on the right-hand side. Well, this was my first impression. If you follow the left footage where you see the Studio B headline and you have the scroll with the running message, and if you follow my voice as you hear it from the footage on the left-hand side, and if you look at the case of the shell on the right-hand side, you will see that it's a small portion of several seconds. Of course, what do you think could have happened and -- in these couple of seconds that -- that would not have been on that other footage, because it was viewed by 28.000 people. So of course you see that by the time it finishes on the left-hand side I only finish my sentence. The raw material cannot be 100 per cent reliable for me, for my purposes, unlike the purposes that you need it for, because as I tell you, I did not have it all the time with me. The left-hand footage shows you how short an interval this is. Could someone have shot or killed someone in these five seconds in that interim? That would have been nonsense. One would have known about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's not the question I was going to ask you or imply that anybody was shot during that gap. My question is as follows: When you look at those two pieces of footage, you start off seeing Mr. Borovcanin talking to people. It pans the camera -- you panned over to the left and you see a pile of belongings and a gate and a goat, and then on your raw material we see the shell casing. On the Studio B material we see the zoom-in shot of the men on the balcony, and just for your information, I don't want to play the whole tape again, but there is nowhere on the raw material where we have the shot from Studio B. I hope what I said is clear. My question is having seen that, do you think that the men on the balcony was taped over with the film of the shell since after this clip they both come back together with a shot of the base and the same man walking?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, this is one of the moments that is missing from the raw material and which was fortunately found when I provided the VHS tape from Canada, which contains all the controversial portions on account of which I had many problems in Serbia, because many people accused me of having erased some much atrocious crimes. We cannot reliably ascertain, and I'm not clairvoyant enough for that, to see what it was, but whatever happened to that raw material, the only relevant original is this tape because it contains all the portions that were believed to have been hidden by me. If you -- if you look at the camera that was used, it had such poor facilities of zooming. Even if I held that frame for five seconds longer, it was the same frame, you need to know that. It shows all those people whom your experts later identified with sophisticated equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never of course never paid any attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll move on --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll move on and move away from the men on the balcony. Now, we've just looked at some footage from Potocari on the 13th, and you've told us how you went there and filmed part of the DutchBat base and that you got out of the car, walked around. We've seen the video. Where did you go next after you and Mr. Borovcanin -- or where did you go next after you left Potocari?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since we were following the chronology of our movement, we -- and went out into the field. As I said, the operations were ongoing. We set out from Bratunac along the road to Tuzla -- or, rather, toward the crossroads where the road forks off to Tuzla and Zvornik. Later on you showed me what it was called, but for years I didn't know what the name of the place was. When I went back with the French TV crew there in 2006, I was absolutely unable to recognise the place where the prisoners were, for instance. It has all changed. Certain houses were destroyed at the time but reconstructed now. At any rate, we set out from the town along the road which had occasionally been used by the columns of buses and trucks ferrying the refugees to Tuzla. That was the part that we first filmed in our news report. At that point we came across those anti-aircraft vehicles. Some call it Praga, but that's not the calibre of the -- I don't think that was the vehicle. That was the footage that I made. What I want you to keep in mind is that the shooting was going on, and something that is not widely known and Mr. Agius should be aware of that, I made that bit of footage when my life was at risk, because we were constantly under fire and that's why the driver was speeding in between the stops that we made, because everybody is convinced -- everybody who is in a war is that if you drive over 120 kilometres an hour that you would survive or manage to avoid getting shot. You have the footage today solely thanks to the fact that nobody hit us at the time. Of course I'm referring to the fire from the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. And then --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And that -- let me show you a map, if we can, and see if that helps you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, I should have the e-court number, but it's our map binder 211, map 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is a map of the area just to see if it helps you remember. If you have any trouble seeing it on the screen, let me know and I'm let you look at my copy. Can you read the names of the places on there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. If you look right about the middle towards the right side we've got Potocari, north to Bratunac, and then a road branching off going through Kravica, Sandici, and up to Konjevic Polje. Take a look at this, you describe the route. See if that helps you remember at all where were you driving with Mr. Borovcanin that day after you left Potocari?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know that's the only road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay just to be clear the road between Bratunac and Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I never got to Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember. And do you know why? That place name was already known for the first massacre against the Serbs committed by Oric in 1993, in the wintertime of 1993. And if I had been there, I would have filmed in Konjevic Polje. It was well-known back in our parts, if it isn't in yours. As I look at the map I see what you refer to as Sandici. I don't recall this junction. Ahead of Konjevic Polje there is a junction forking off to Kasaba, that's the road to Sarajevo. And to the right is the road to Zvornik and on to Serbia. So that's roughly it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. If you remember roughly where did this constant firing that you experienced on this road start? I mean, how close to Bratunac? The firing from the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard, but I can't be precise, beyond Bratunac. Several kilometres beyond Bratunac towards Glogova. We were heading in the direction of Zvornik, and the fire came from the right-hand side. You could see the Kravica rivulet or a creek if I remember correctly. So to the left of that, if we're heading towards Zvornik, to the left is that rivulet and then the headland on the hills, and throughout the area there was shooting. I recall us stopping from time to time because certain sections of the road were unsafe because there was gunfire, and they were unsafe for the buses to go through. The situation prevailed as such throughout the day. This showed me that the Serbs did not achieve a victory there since the Muslims continued fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it was pretty soon that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you recall whether the convoys of buses and trucks with the people you described as refugees on them were stopped at any time during that day? The same time you were there when there was firing.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that this was the case on -- on two or three occasions, that there were two or three stops, perhaps half an hour. You know how it is in time of war. There are certain zones that are dangerous, but they cease to be dangerous as certain forces are pushed back, and the civilians have to wait because they should not be exposed to fire. Of course, this rule did not apply to me. We pressed on, under fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand. Now, when you went back and said that you couldn't find any of the places along this road, the famous footage you shot of the front of what we call the Kravica warehouse of the bodies, were you able to find that building with the French camera crew?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't recall that I could, because on the other side -- well, you see, ten years later the landscape is quite different. There are many new homes built. The old ones that were wrecked may have been destroyed. At the time, there were many destroyed homes that had been torched and demolished by Oric's men in 1993, and of course it is impossible for one to speak with any reliability on that later on. Besides, I only made several seconds worth of footage of that, two or three seconds only.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Last question before we -- we have to have a break for the interpreters and to change tapes during this part of the trip you described, if you remember, if you remember, were you alone with Borovcanin in the car or was there a driver?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe the driver was there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I don't think there's anything that I can -- if we're going to stop at 3.45, I'd rather stop now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Before we break, Mr. McCloskey, there is another motion from the Miletic Defence team to have present their military advisor during the testimony of Richard Butler. Do you have any objections? It's similar to the Pandurevic motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So the motion is granted for the same reasons as explained before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To avoid any confusion, I place at everyone's disposal my papers here as in your warning before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You can take them with you. No one has asked for them as yet. We'll deal with that if there is a special ad hoc request. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much more are you --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think I'll finish in the next session. It has taken me a little longer than I thought and I'll try to move it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I'll ask you, sir, if you can, to keep your answers as short as you can while still answering the questions, just so that we don't keep you longer than we have to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record I notice the presence of Mr. Haynes now in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. We were talking a little bit about -- I think you mentioned the Pragas and the firing into the hills. I want to show you a clip from 2054. Not a clip, a segment. This is your raw material which you provided to us, and the part I'm interested in - I didn't show this earlier - is there is a black frame. There appears to be a little piece missing in this sequence, and we're starting at 12:17:1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And the blank space of a few seconds started at 12:41. I'll just ask you, if you can, if you don't know, if you don't remember that's okay, but do you know what -- why there's that gap there on the raw material?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see a gap.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, where the screen goes black.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, the answer's the same. This is my universal answer for all the situation of that kind in the raw material, because it's obvious that you want to talk about the raw material more than the programme that I actually aired. I really cannot give you any reasons. Especially here you can see that the fire's being opened from a PAT [Realtime transcript read in error "path"] onto a hill from which the Muslims are firing. I really did not pay any attention to that. I didn't even pay attention to the dialogue that went on. I did not pay attention to that because I was filming. As for the things that they're saying I really -- what I'm saying is I was focused on the image. And as for the gap, I really don't have any answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just one small correction for the transcript. It's on page 38, line 20. It does say "firing is being opened from a path onto a hill" but this is not a word, pat. It should read "PAT" which means in our language "anti-aircraft gun."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I suppose you confirm this, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. This is a military abbreviation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The transcript will be corrected accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to now play a short clip --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Nicholls, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: My microphone is flashing. I don't know if --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we can now play a short clip of the same time from Studio B, video 2011.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We're at 8:36:2 and also to be precise we can see that the counter on the original tape is at 16:48:00. That is what is on the screen of the Studio B tape. This part of the footage of your Studio B, you will have to take my word for it without playing the entire tape, is not on your raw material, and can you tell us, if you know, why this is gone, and I think your answer -- if your answer's just the same, then that's fine.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer's the same. In the text I even made a mistake. I said that these were Pragas, which I've simply misspoke. It's a slip of the tongue. It was actually a PAT.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We'll finish this clip. [Videotape played]?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, when you shot these bits we've seen of the PATs, as you call them, firing into the hills, were you inside or outside of the car?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I am -- I am on side of -- [Interpretation] I was next to the car, which is proven by the music that you can hear, something that you can't possibly link with the situation of that story. The radio was on in the car, and even in this dangerous situation, i.e., it would have been normal for me to have a flak jacket like any American journalist would have. An American journalist does not leave a car without a flak jacket, and I didn't have one. They could have opened fire. I could have been killed. That was a theoretical possibility. As soon as we pulled over, I got out of the car on the right-hand side. I was on the right-hand side in the back, and I was shooting from there because I wanted to have as best shot as possible. That's why you can hear this music coming from the car radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I want to show you one photo. This will only take a second. It's 2986, the Road Book Exhibit, page 52. Photo B is the one I'm interested in. This is a still photo from your raw video, sir. All right. If you look at this photo for a second. Again, page 52, photo B we're looking at on the screen now. If you look at the silver/grey car that's farther away from as you took this film, does that spark your memory about anything?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that this is possibly a Golf. There were a lot of Golf cars in Yugoslavia at the time. As I'm looking at the photo, but it doesn't remind me of anything. If you're implying I that might have ridden in that car I really can't remember. It may have been that car, but I don't know what car it was, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. You made that very clear. Thank you. I want to show you another bit of video now and ask you a question about it. This is -- actually, first -- we can just play the video. That's fine. This is from the raw video again, 2011. We're at 21:00:9.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. We stopped at 22:57:05.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: First of all --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. First of all do you remember shooting this sequence? Did it stick in your mind at all, these people surrendering out of the woods?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were coming from the woods, and then they were descending towards the little river that showed to me on the map, and then they surrendered, and then they came up to the road, to the house. As far as I can remember, they passed by their house. That's where you get to the road, and then from there you get to that meadow where I shot the sequence. This is the sequence. I don't know what else you want to know. When I'm watching this video again, yeah, it all comes back to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The young man we see in the frame here, 22:57:5, which just for the record is very similar to page 56, photo E of 2986, do you remember what happened to him shortly after you filmed him on this day? Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you see him and the other of this group of boys get onto the bus that day which took them to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that, because when the text was published in The Times in 1998 I was shocked because my memory was still fresh. I repeat, I saw him with a group of young men or children under the age of 18 more or less entering a bus or entering the lorries, I don't know who got on where. In any case, they got on the vehicles and ended up in Tuzla. This was not the case of a successful escape owing to a body of water or a well behind which he hid and then he went to Tuzla. This is a nonsense. But let me help you with something else if I may --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. Wait for the question, please, and if you need to add that you can, if the Court permits me to say that. At the time that this boy and the other boys were separated from the older men as you've described it and put on a bus to take them to Tuzla, who -- who, if anyone, made the order that that should happen, or said that that should happen?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who issued the order for them to get on the bus?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, Mr. Borovcanin, when we arrived there at first saw that there were young men there who could not have been soldiers, and as far as I can remember, he said immediately that the transport of refugees should be stopped and that these boys should be sent to Tuzla. It's very difficult for me to quote his very words, but that was more or less what happened. That was the situation. We arrived together, so he saw the same things that I saw myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you remember, did Mr. Borovcanin, after deciding that these boys should be put on a bus and go to Tuzla, did he stop the bus himself or did somebody else do that, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I don't know what I told you in the interview in Belgrade, but in my view it is really not important. I know for a fact that they were transported from that meadow in buses. I don't know whether it was one of the guards. I suppose it was one of them, because Borovcanin was observing the overall situation. There were people by the road. I don't remember him stopping for any longer in that place. But if you will allow me --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session for a short while, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, without mentioning any names, please, Mr. Pirocanac, you've -- you've told us about a different research you've done, and you've checked into facts and you knew about the lists. Do you know what happened to the other men on the meadow captured that day?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Really, this is not information that a journalist could get in middle of operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I mean now do you know?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, even now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rumours that some of them were -- pardon. [Interpretation] I apologise. I apologise once again. This was in 1995, and then rumours about the events in Srebrenica spread. So I might have heard some whether they were killed, but I did not get that officially. This would be information -- information from the local international media. I know about a man called Ramo, who is also used in the Panorama. I shot him as well, and scene was very distressing. Somebody told me about him. Maybe somebody from BBC, from that team, that this man had been killed, and I remember him, and I remember having heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. But now -- now -- this is my last question on the topic. As you sit here today, having followed some of the trials in this Tribunal and the information you all possess today, were men taken from that meadow that you filmed and killed? Do you think that's -- based on all your information is that right or is that still just a rumour?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was there, nobody moved from the place but the children that got on the buses. But can I ask you something in return, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, I'm afraid you can't. That's not part of the rules?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can we go into private session for one minute?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's not up to me, Your Honours, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, you are right. You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: After court when this is all done you can ask me anything you want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now I want to move to a new topic. This is something you discussed in your article and also in our interview. I'm moving up to asking you questions about the -- the very dramatic footage you shot of the dead bodies in front of that warehouse, but first I want you to tell us what you recall, what you heard on that day, 13 July, about somebody named Officer, that nickname. Tell us what you heard, briefly if you can, what you heard and when you heard it.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case, this was during the period of time when we left Bratunac and filmed everybody on the road, the group of detainees and the rest. It was during that period of time. I can't tell you exactly when. I was an external observer, I could see that something had happened, and my final conclusion based on the information when we reached the hospital where we went was that one fighter under the command of Mr. Borovcanin whose nickname was Officer had been wounded, that he had jumped on somebody who had weapons, and that his arms were hurt in that skirmish, and that he had been urgently transported to the hospital in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember whom you heard this from?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I suppose that there must have been a conversation between Borovcanin and somebody who had told him that, or maybe he heard it over the Motorola. My memory on that is very vague. The detail was not important. I mean, it was important because the man got hurt, which means that Serbs also suffered, not only Muslims, and they had problems as well as the Muslims, but I don't know what the man's name was and what the situation was, but I know that as soon as he got the news we headed urgently towards Bratunac. And again fire was opened from the right-hand side where I was, from where I was filming.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
